topic: Sharp policy-update budget frontier for adaptive Neyman allocation. For n binary Gaussian experimental units, exact-count batches with treatment share in [1/4,3/4], compact nondegenerate arm-variance box, and deterministic normalized weights on batchwise mean differences, define the exactly-B normalized excess-MSE frontier above the constrained oracle variance. Characterize it for every 1<=B<=floor(n/4), derive the at-most-B lower envelope and operational saturation regime, prove matching adaptive schedules and chronological information lower bounds, solve the one- and two-batch anchors, and derive a variance estimator, CLT, and fixed-time Wald coverage. The Amazon adaptive-abtester update cadence is the consumer. PRESOLVE EVIDENCE REQUIRING VERIFICATION: the exact risk decomposition reduces design loss to batch-weight mismatch plus allocation regret; adaptive Fisher information, van Trees, grid quantization, and harmonic weight optimization support Psi_exact,B asymptotic to B((n+1)^(1/B)-1)/n+(B/n)^2. A legal square-root pilot attains the matching two-batch exponent, while B=n/4 reveals a genuine exact-batch overscheduling penalty; the at-most-B envelope reaches order log(n)/n. UNRESOLVED BOTTLENECK: prove the sharp chronological Gaussian learning constant and matching logarithmic-batch construction needed for the literal factor-two saturation threshold; rate bounds alone do not settle that constant. EARLY KILL TEST: on sigma(theta)=(s exp(theta),s exp(-theta)), derive exact adaptive-history information 2T and test whether one smooth prior yields the claimed sharp cumulative allocation-loss coefficient; failure pivots the factor-two claim to an unspecified constant-factor threshold. STRONGEST-FORM DRAFT (unverified, gaps listed inside): <repo-root>/internal/presolve_drafts/exp_update_budget_neyman_frontier.md.

open_problems.open_problem: Determine the sharp minimax exactly-B normalized excess-MSE frontier for every integer 1 <= B <= floor(n/4) in binary Gaussian adaptive Neyman experiments with exact within-batch counts, constrained treatment shares, compact arm variances, and deterministic normalized weights.

source_refs.claim: The paper gives logarithmic-batch constructions and a second-order rate for linear causal functionals, but not a sharp frontier indexed by every fixed update budget.
source_refs.author: Jiachun Li and David Simchi-Levi

source_refs.claim: The paper formulates multistage variance learning as adaptive Neyman allocation and reports an algorithm that almost matches, rather than exactly attains, its information-theoretic limit.
source_refs.author: Jinglong Zhao

source_refs.claim: For reward regret, the paper derives batch-number-dependent upper and lower rates using adaptive grids, demonstrating a nontrivial feedback-budget frontier under a different loss.
source_refs.author: Zijun Gao, Yanjun Han, Zhimei Ren, and Zhengqing Zhou

open_problems.why_unsolved: The closest adaptive-Neyman results establish first-order efficiency benchmarks, second-order approach rates, or near-information-theoretic guarantees, but they do not solve the decision problem conditional on each exact integer B with integer treatment counts and a fixed weighted estimator. Batched-bandit frontiers instead minimize reward regret through mean-gap testing; transferring their machinery requires replacing that testing problem by chronological learning of the variance ratio while also controlling allocation regret and batch-weight mismatch.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: A uniform asymptotic equivalent or exact finite-n variational characterization of Psi_exact,B(n), with explicit B=1 and B=2 anchors, a feasible B-batch schedule attaining the leading constant, and a chronological-information lower bound with the same constant.

writing_exemplar.why: Its introduction treats policy updates as an operationally costly resource and converts that deployment constraint into an efficiency question.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Per-unit adaptation is costly and unstable -> batching makes platform experiments implementable -> one must quantify how quickly batching approaches the oracle -> the destination is the sharp frontier at every update budget B.

method_exemplars.technique: Use sequential limit-experiment representations and endogenous-information-set factorization to characterize attainable distributions under chronological decisions, then optimize the induced Gaussian risk.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The required lower bound ranges over all chronological B-stage designs, the adaptive decision class their representation theorem is designed to reduce.

method_exemplars.technique: Adapt the Neyman-regret-to-estimator-variance decomposition and conservative variance-estimation proof from per-unit updates to batchwise exact-count decisions.
method_exemplars.why_closest: It studies the same ATE precision benchmark and supplies adaptive allocation and Wald-facing machinery, but does not impose a finite update budget.

method_exemplars.technique: Adapt the recursively spaced batch grid and change-of-measure lower-bound tree, replacing arm-mean alternatives by nearby Gaussian variance-ratio alternatives.
method_exemplars.why_closest: It provides the closest sharp analysis of how finitely many chronological feedback rounds change an adaptive decision problem.

open_problems.open_problem: Establish the sharp chronological Gaussian learning constant for cumulative allocation loss on the local path sigma_1(theta)=s exp(theta), sigma_0(theta)=s exp(-theta), under B-stage exact-count policies.

source_refs.claim: The paper constructs limit experiments for multistage adaptive experiments and characterizes attainable limit distributions under endogenous information sets.
source_refs.author: Keisuke Hirano and Jack R. Porter

source_refs.claim: The paper proves first-order efficiency lower bounds under assignments that may depend on covariates and past outcomes, with optimized propensities recovering the Neyman benchmark.
source_refs.author: Timothy B. Armstrong

source_refs.claim: The paper supplies an average-propensity lower bound and a second-order rate, but not the local cumulative-learning constant needed for a literal update-budget threshold.
source_refs.author: Jiachun Li and David Simchi-Levi

open_problems.why_unsolved: First-order efficiency bounds collapse an adaptive design to an average propensity and therefore discard when variance information became available. The desired constant is chronological and second-order because observations from a batch cannot repair that batch's allocation error. Existing sequential limit-experiment machinery must be strengthened to preserve the predictable information process for theta and to prove a Bayes or local-minimax inequality for cumulative pre-update allocation loss rather than terminal estimator variance alone.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: A verified local asymptotic minimax theorem on the stated Gaussian path computing the exact leading constant in the infimum of expected cumulative squared Neyman-share error over chronological B-stage policies, together with an attaining policy or a counterexample showing that the conjectured factor-two saturation constant is false.

writing_exemplar.why: It frames unknown arm variances as the information bottleneck preventing direct implementation of oracle Neyman allocation.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Oracle allocation requires unknown variances -> early outcomes reveal their ratio -> later policies can use only previously revealed information -> the destination is the exact chronological price of learning that ratio.

method_exemplars.technique: Derive the local Gaussian experiment batch by batch while preserving endogenous information sets, then use the representation theorem to restrict possible policy-estimator limits.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The sought constant is a local minimax quantity over adaptive chronological experiments, precisely the class represented by this paper.

method_exemplars.technique: Adapt the least-favorable parametric submodel and score-information calculation used to lower-bound regular ATE estimators under adaptive assignment.
method_exemplars.why_closest: Its proof already permits assignment based on past outcomes; the new step is retaining stage timing and second-order allocation loss.

open_problems.open_problem: Solve the finite-n and sharp-asymptotic two-batch Gaussian Neyman design problem by jointly optimizing the exact-count pilot size, pilot allocation, second-batch plug-in rule, and deterministic aggregation weights over a compact nondegenerate variance box.

source_refs.claim: With a fixed pilot size, feasible Neyman allocation can have higher asymptotic variance than balanced randomization, especially near homoskedasticity or under high kurtosis.
source_refs.author: Yong Cai and Ahnaf Rafi

source_refs.claim: The paper uses first-wave data to select a second-wave propensity minimizing an asymptotic ATE variance bound under consistently learned design inputs.
source_refs.author: Jinyong Hahn, Keisuke Hirano, and Dean Karlan

source_refs.claim: The paper develops a two-wave batch-adaptive Neyman design, unbiased estimation, inference, and practical pilot guidance rather than a sharp minimax pilot-size constant.
source_refs.author: Matthew Blackwell, Nicole E. Pashley, and Dominic Valentino

open_problems.why_unsolved: The two-wave literature divides between large-pilot asymptotics, fixed-pilot warnings, and practical pilot guidance. It does not jointly optimize a sublinear pilot while accounting for exact integer counts, constrained allocation shares, and the contribution of both waves through deterministic weights. The missing proof step is a uniform expansion balancing pilot opportunity cost against inverse-chi-square error in the learned Gaussian variance ratio.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: An exact finite-n minimax characterization or sharp uniform asymptotic expansion for B=2 identifying the optimal pilot order and leading constant, optimal second-wave rule and weights, and the variance-ratio region where adaptation beats balanced one-batch randomization.

writing_exemplar.why: Its motivation centers on the practically important mismatch between ideal large pilots and the small pilots researchers actually possess.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Neyman allocation is efficient with known variances -> real pilots estimate variances noisily -> plug-in allocation can be worse than balance -> the destination is the optimally sized and weighted two-batch design.

method_exemplars.technique: Adapt the mixture-limit calculation for random plug-in propensities and the second-order analysis of the variance-ratio estimator to a growing pilot using exact Gaussian moments.
method_exemplars.why_closest: It directly quantifies the precision penalty generated by noisy pilot variance estimates.

method_exemplars.technique: Carry over the two-stage propensity optimization and influence-function variance calculation while retaining the first wave in the final optimally weighted estimator.
method_exemplars.why_closest: It is the canonical econometric two-stage design for learning a variance-minimizing treatment probability.

method_exemplars.technique: Use exact discrete marginal variance gains instead of rounded continuous Neyman shares when optimizing both batches' integer counts.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The requested design has exact counts, and this paper isolates the failure of rounded Neyman allocations even in the static oracle problem.

open_problems.open_problem: Characterize the at-most-B lower envelope of the exactly-B Neyman excess-MSE frontiers and locate its sharp saturation threshold, including whether forcing B near n/4 creates an overscheduling penalty relative to using fewer updates.

source_refs.claim: The paper shows that logarithmically many batches suffice to approach its efficiency benchmark, but does not optimize over every allowed update count or compare exactly-B with at-most-B policies.
source_refs.author: Jiachun Li and David Simchi-Levi

source_refs.claim: The paper obtains an anytime near-logarithmic Neyman-regret guarantee under bounded finite-population outcomes, but updates sequentially and does not price policy revisions.
source_refs.author: Georgy Noarov, Riccardo Fogliato, Martin Bertran, and Aaron Roth

source_refs.claim: The paper establishes a batch-dependent minimax reward-regret frontier and shows that few batches can approach fully sequential performance.
source_refs.author: Vianney Perchet, Philippe Rigollet, Sylvain Chassang, and Erik Snowberg

open_problems.why_unsolved: Available Neyman-allocation papers prove sequential regret rates or exhibit a logarithmic-batch construction, but do not distinguish the nonmonotone exactly-B constraint from the monotone at-most-B decision problem. The first proof step that changes from batched-bandit saturation arguments is the loss decomposition: extra mandatory batches can force small exact-count cells and unfavorable deterministic aggregation weights even after feedback has little remaining learning value, invalidating the usual monotonicity intuition.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: A characterization of Psi_at-most,B(n)=min_{1<=b<=B} Psi_exact,b(n), its minimizing effective batch count and sharp saturation threshold, together with matching lower and upper bounds for the excess cost of compulsory overscheduling.

writing_exemplar.why: It presents update frequency as an operational resource rather than an asymptotic technicality.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Platforms cannot revise policies continuously -> logarithmically many revisions may recover efficiency -> operators still must choose a cadence -> the destination is the at-most-B envelope and its saturation point.

method_exemplars.technique: Transfer optimized batch-grid recursions and adaptive-grid lower bounds to the learned variance-ratio state.
method_exemplars.why_closest: Its main object is explicitly a performance frontier indexed by the number of feedback batches, although under reward regret.

method_exemplars.technique: Use strong convexity of Neyman loss to convert squared allocation error into excess variance, aggregating only over selected update epochs.
method_exemplars.why_closest: That conversion is the natural upper-bound bridge from learned variance ratios to the at-most-B excess-MSE envelope.

method_exemplars.technique: Use the exact marginal-variance decomposition for integer allocations to isolate the lattice cost created by compulsory small batches.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The predicted overscheduling effect is partly an integrality phenomenon, and rounded continuous Neyman allocations need not minimize variance.

open_problems.open_problem: Prove a variance estimator, uniform CLT, and fixed-time Wald coverage result for a frontier-attaining exact-count batch estimator when the number of batches ranges from fixed B through the logarithmic saturation regime.

source_refs.claim: The paper proves Batched OLS asymptotic normality for a fixed number of batches as observations per batch diverge and shows ordinary OLS can be nonnormal under adaptive allocation.
source_refs.author: Kelly W. Zhang, Lucas Janson, and Susan A. Murphy

source_refs.claim: The paper proves a fixed-sample CLT and semiparametric efficiency for adaptive AIPW under changing assignment policies and constructs fixed-time and anytime-valid intervals.
source_refs.author: Thomas Cook, Alan Mishler, and Aaditya Ramdas
source_refs.venue: Conference on Causal Learning and Reasoning

source_refs.claim: For batched adaptive experiments, the paper derives optimal conditional inference given realized stopping, assignment probabilities, and targets.
source_refs.author: Jiafeng Chen and Isaiah Andrews

source_refs.claim: The paper constructs a conservative variance estimator and asymptotically valid intervals for a fully sequential adaptive Neyman design.
source_refs.author: Jessica Dai, Paula Gradu, and Christopher Harshaw

open_problems.why_unsolved: BOLS theory fixes the number of batches and lets every batch grow, while sequential AIPW and Clip-OGD use per-unit randomization and estimator-specific adaptive weights. A frontier schedule can have highly unequal exact-count batches and B=B_n growing logarithmically, so fixed-B independent-stage arguments and existing martingale CLTs do not directly supply uniform Lindeberg control. Exact treatment totals also create within-batch dependence, and the variance estimator must reproduce the deterministic cross-batch weights that attain the MSE frontier.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: A ratio-consistent observable variance estimator and a studentized N(0,1) limit uniformly over the compact Gaussian variance box and admissible frontier schedules with B_n through the saturation order, implying uniform fixed-time 1-alpha Wald coverage.

writing_exemplar.why: It begins with industrial batched adaptation, explains why naive normal inference fails, and formulates a batch-native inferential remedy.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Platforms deploy batched adaptive rules -> adaptation can destroy ordinary asymptotics -> batchwise normalization restores inference -> the destination is validity for the MSE-optimal update-budget schedule.

method_exemplars.technique: Adapt precision-equalized aggregation of conditionally normal batch contrasts and batchwise studentization to exact treatment counts and frontier-optimal deterministic weights.
method_exemplars.why_closest: Its estimator is already built from batch-level treatment-control contrasts, matching the proposed sufficient statistics.

method_exemplars.technique: Use predictable quadratic-variation stabilization and martingale CLT arguments, with truncation supplied by the treatment-share constraint.
method_exemplars.why_closest: It provides a strong modern fixed-time adaptive-experiment CLT and variance-estimation template.

method_exemplars.technique: Condition on realized batchwise assignment probabilities and exploit location invariance to separate allocation adaptation from the treatment-effect parameter.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The Gaussian exact-count setting is structurally compatible with their conditional sufficient-statistic reduction.

literature_map:
Neyman (1934) supplies the infeasible oracle: treatment counts proportional to arm standard deviations minimize difference-in-means variance.
Hahn, Hirano, and Karlan (2011, JBES) learn a variance-minimizing propensity in a two-stage experiment, establishing the canonical econometric motivation but not a finite update-budget frontier.
Cai and Rafi (2024, Journal of Econometrics) show that a noisy fixed-size pilot can make feasible Neyman allocation worse than balanced randomization, particularly near homoskedasticity or with high kurtosis.
Blackwell, Pashley, and Valentino (2023) develop batch-adaptive Neyman allocation, unbiased estimation, inference, and practical pilot guidance for social-science experiments.
Zhao (current arXiv version 2026) studies competitive multistage adaptive Neyman allocation and reports an almost-matching rather than exact information-theoretic guarantee.
Dai, Gradu, and Harshaw (NeurIPS 2023) define Neyman regret, obtain a near-square-root design-based guarantee through Clip-OGD, and provide conservative variance estimation and Wald intervals.
Neopane, Ramdas, and Singh (2024) obtain logarithmic superpopulation Neyman regret; Noarov, Fogliato, Bertran, and Roth (ICML 2025) obtain near-logarithmic anytime design-based regret under stronger boundedness.
Kato, Ishihara, Honda, and Narita and Cook, Mishler, and Ramdas establish semiparametrically efficient adaptive AIPW estimation and fixed-time or anytime-valid inference.
Hadad, Hirshberg, Zhan, Wager, and Athey (PNAS 2021) show why naive estimators can be biased or heavy-tailed under adaptive sampling and use variance-stabilizing adaptive weights.
Zhang, Janson, and Murphy (NeurIPS 2020) show ordinary OLS can be nonnormal in batched bandits and obtain BOLS normality under a fixed-number-of-batches asymptotic.
Armstrong (2022) and Hirano and Porter (2023) provide first-order efficiency bounds and limit-experiment representations for general adaptive or multistage designs, supplying natural machinery for chronological lower bounds.
Li and Simchi-Levi (2026) give an average-propensity lower bound, logarithmic-batch constructions, and a second-order rate for linear causal functionals, but not an every-B exact-count frontier with a matched leading constant.
Perchet et al. (COLT 2016) and Gao et al. (NeurIPS 2019) show that reward-regret frontiers depend sharply on feedback batches; their geometric grids and change-of-measure trees optimize a different loss.
Wright (Statistics & Probability Letters 2017) proves that rounded continuous Neyman shares need not be integer-optimal, isolating a lattice issue for exact-count adaptive experiments.
The scan located no paper jointly characterizing exactly-B versus at-most-B excess MSE, its sharp saturation constant, exact counts, and growing-B Wald inference; this conjunction is the live research boundary.
